title: Connector architecture sync - LumenAI
header: Date: 2026-01-22 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m\nLocation: Zoom | Recording: yes | Redwood: Alex Monroe (AE), Priya Singh (SE) | LumenAI: Daniel Kim (CTO), Sara Ortiz (Platform), Maya Patel (Data)
summary: Introductory architecture sync between Redwood AE/SE and LumenAI platform team to evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private for their production chat and retrieval augmentation pipeline. Discussed SDK options (REST/SDK), LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits and quota enforcement, observability hooks and benchmarking plan. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a small throughput latency benchmark, LumenAI to share sample prompts and traffic profile, follow-up technical deep dive next week.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Gateway/proxy patterns and sidecar vs external proxy
Rate limiting / quotas and token accounting
Observability hooks / tracing / token-level cost breakdown
Security: VPC, KMS, SOC2 and audit logs
action_items: Priya Singh: Run baseline throughput + p95 latency benchmark using LumenAI sample dataset (due 2026-01-29)
Daniel Kim: Share 7-day traffic profile, sample prompt set and privacy requirements (due 2026-01-25)
Alex Monroe: Send pricing for hosted vs dedicated options and security pack details (due 2026-01-24)
next_steps: Schedule technical deep dive (SE-led) to review benchmark results and integration code (target 2026-01-29)
Exchange sample prompt set and S3 access for benchmark dataset
Priya to provide a small Redwood test project (LangChain example) for LumenAI to try in their dev env
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we put together like a 45 minute agenda, we can stretch to an hour. Intro from both sides?
[00:06] Daniel Kim: Yep, Daniel here, CTO at LumenAI, we run a chat+retrieval product internally and evaluating Redwood for inference serving.
[00:12] Sara Ortiz: Sara, platform eng, I'll be the integration owner, mostly worried about networking and quotas.
[00:16] Maya Patel: Maya, DS, I'll bring the prompt sets and evaluation metrics.
[00:20] Priya Singh: Priya from Redwood, SE, I focus on latency, batching, and SDK integrations, happy to go deep.
[00:28] Alex Monroe: Cool. High-level goal - LumenAI needs predictable latency for chat (p95 < 300ms for short prompts) and cost control for large embedding jobs. Also need on-prem options for certain customers.
[00:38] Daniel Kim: Exactly. We have three buckets: low-latency chat, bulk embed pipelines, and a few regulated enterprise tenants that require private deployment. We're trying to figure out if hosted + VPC peering can work or if we need dedicated or private deployments.
[00:51] Priya Singh: Great. Quick overview: Redwood offerings — hosted API for fast onboarding, dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and private deployments (VPC/on-prem) for regulated workloads. From an integration perspective there are two common patterns: direct SDK (Rust/Go/Python) calls to Redwood host, or run a gateway/proxy in front for routing, rate-limits, and local caching.
[01:12] Sara Ortiz: On the gateway topic, we already run a sidecar pattern in other services. Curious about recommended approach: sidecar per service vs centralized external proxy. What are tradeoffs?
[01:22] Priya Singh: Good question. Sidecar gives local caching (prefix + KV cache) and minimizes network hop for KV lookups, helps with low latency. Centralized proxy simplifies routing and enforcement across teams and is easier for quotas and SSO. But centralized can be a single point to scale and you need to handle burst capacity. Redwood supports both — we provide proxy image and SDKs.
[01:40] Maya Patel: How does the KV cache work with LlamaIndex flows? We're worried about stale keys and consistency with reranks.
[01:47] Priya Singh: For LlamaIndex, we typically integrate at the retriever layer. The cache keys are deterministic by prompt+context hash, and Redwood's cache TTLs are configurable per-route. There is some nuance with streaming and incremental tokens — cache hits avoid recomputing KV state so you save on latency.
[02:05] Daniel Kim: On rate limits: we have per-tenant quotas and want to enforce per-user daily limits as well. Does Redwood let us push quota decisions to our side or does it have to be server-side?
[02:15] Alex Monroe: Redwood has token-level accounting in the control plane and you can enforce quotas at multiple levels: per API key, per-customer, or per-route. You can also have your sidecar reject requests before they hit Redwood. Many customers implement a hybrid: local enforcement for quick rejections and server-side accounting for billing/observability.
[02:34] Sara Ortiz: Observability hooks — we need traces that correlate our request IDs with token usage and model latency. What's available?
[02:40] Priya Singh: We have per-request tracing headers you can pass through (x-redwood-trace-id), and the console shows token-level breakdowns, model time vs network time, and per-route p50/p95. You can push logs to your SIEM via syslog/forwarder or pull from audit logs. We also expose a lightweight OpenTelemetry-compatible exporter.
[02:58] Maya Patel: Nice. For LangChain / LlamaIndex, do you have example connectors or adapters?
[03:03] Priya Singh: Yes, we maintain example repos. For LangChain we have a small "RedwoodLLM" wrapper that fits as an LLM in LangChain, and for LlamaIndex we have an adapter that wraps remote embedding/llm calls. We can share a sample project that runs locally and points to hosted Redwood endpoints.
[03:20] Daniel Kim: Great, can we run one of those in our staging cluster behind our proxy and push traffic?
[03:25] Priya Singh: Absolutely. We'll provide the example and you can swap in your API key. For dedicated or private deployments we'd ship a connector image so you can run it inside your VPC.
[03:34] Sara Ortiz: Security: SOC2 is fine, but what about KMS/HSM integration for private? Some of our customers want keys not held by Redwood.
[03:41] Alex Monroe: Under private we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations and HSM for the on-prem package. For hosted, we do managed keys but can add envelope encryption and key rotation policies; for enterprises we offer options in the private deployment contract.
[03:56] Maya Patel: Latency vs cost question — embedding large corpora is expensive. Do you recommend quantization/LLM selection per workload?
[04:03] Priya Singh: Yes. We suggest different model profiles: smaller quantized models for bulk embeddings and retriever steps, larger models for generation where quality is critical. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization and batching configs from a short trace of your workload. Batching and prefix caching reduce per-token cost while maintaining latency SLOs.
[04:23] Daniel Kim: Can Redwood do canary rollouts and automatic fallback if a model variant fails?
[04:28] Priya Singh: Yes, rollout policies in the console: canary percentage, A/B, automatic fallback to a compatible variant or older version, and circuit-breaking rules. That helps keep production serving stable during model updates.
[04:40] Sara Ortiz: On quotas again, what about rate shaping for bursty traffic — can we set token-per-second caps and burst windows per route?
[04:48] Alex Monroe: Yes, rate shaping is per-route and supports a token bucket model with configurable burst capacity. You can also set prioritization rules so certain enterprise tenants get preferential throughput.
[04:57] Maya Patel: About observability: can I see token attribution to particular prompt templates or user sessions? We need this for debugging hallucinations tied to prompt changes.
[05:06] Priya Singh: You can annotate requests with metadata (prompt_template_id, session_id) and that flows through to the token breakdown. The console and APIs let you filter traces by metadata. For long-term regression tracking we tie evals to prompt sets and alert on quality drift.
[05:22] Daniel Kim: Network topology — for private tenants on AWS, can Redwood sit in our VPC or do we have to host the runtime?
[05:30] Priya Singh: Both options. For private customers, we offer a customer-managed control plane where the runtime can be deployed into your VPC using our Helm charts or an on-prem package. For dedicated we run the runtime in our infra but can provide VPC peering and private connectivity.
[05:46] Sara Ortiz: Any gotchas with egress limits when embedding? We have a lot of S3 access patterns during preprocessing.
[05:52] Priya Singh: Preprocessing on your side is typical — run batch embedding jobs in your infra and call Redwood for inference or embeddings depending on model selection. If you send large payloads we recommend chunking and streaming to reduce memory and to get incremental results.
[06:07] Maya Patel: Okay, can we talk about a small benchmark plan? What metrics should we capture?
[06:11] Priya Singh: Capture p50/p95/p99 latency for typical prompt sizes (short chat vs long document retrieval), throughput (tokens/sec), model cost per 1k tokens, and error rate. Also measure end-to-end user-perceived latency including gateway and network hops. We'll run the same workload on hosted and dedicated to compare.
[06:28] Alex Monroe: We'll scope a 2-hour benchmark run — give us a representative 500-1k prompt set and traffic pattern. Priya will spin up the workload and we can share results in a spreadsheet.
[06:36] Daniel Kim: Sounds good. A few operational questions — how do you handle query replay or audit logs for compliance?
[06:43] Priya Singh: Audit logs are retained per your contract; private deployments let you keep logs in your S3 or SIEM. We also provide redact rules and tokenization hooks if you need to strip PII before logs are stored.
[06:56] Sara Ortiz: For the SDKs — our stack is primarily Go and Python. Are both official supported?
[07:01] Priya Singh: Yes, official SDKs for Python, Go, and Node. We also have a small Rust community SDK. The SDKs support streaming, function call semantics, and automatic retry/backoff with jitter.
[07:12] Daniel Kim: Does the SDK expose low-level rate-limit headers so we can implement client-side retry/backoff?
[07:16] Priya Singh: Yes, the SDK surfaces rate-limit headers and max-token windows. You can hook into our retry policy, or override it to apply your own.
[07:24] Maya Patel: Anything about billing visibility? We want per-tenant cost breakdowns for internal chargeback.
[07:29] Alex Monroe: Console offers token-level billing by API key, route, or tenant tag. We can also export usage reports daily to your billing bucket.
[07:37] Sara Ortiz: Is there a way to split costs between model compute and network? We need that for our FinOps team.
[07:42] Priya Singh: The cost breakdown shows model compute vs inference runtime vs egress. For dedicated customers we can give more granular telemetry.
[07:50] Daniel Kim: Any integration examples with LangChain for multi-step chains and tools? We sometimes call external retrieval + LLM + reranker.
[07:59] Priya Singh: Our LangChain example shows a chain that calls a remote retriever, remote LLM, and a local reranker. We support function/tool calling patterns with structured JSON outputs and streaming. The example includes a LlamaIndex-style indexer that persists to your vector DB.
[08:16] Maya Patel: If we decide to go dedicated, how long is the lead time?
[08:20] Alex Monroe: Typically 2-4 weeks to provision capacity depending on region and GPU type, can be faster with committed contracts. Private on-prem has longer timelines (4-8 weeks) for helm packaging and validation.
[08:31] Daniel Kim: Ok. For proof-of-concept, we prefer starting hosted then move to dedicated if throughput+compliance requirements justify it. Does that path work?
[08:39] Priya Singh: That's our most common path. Start hosted to validate payloads and prompt engineering, then if you need predictable latency and isolation move to dedicated. Private is usually for regulated tenants.
[08:50] Sara Ortiz: One more question — autoscaling behavior on dedicated, can it burst to additional pools?
[08:55] Priya Singh: Yes, dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity to our shared pool if enabled. You set thresholds and cooldowns.
[09:03] Daniel Kim: Perfect. Any blockers we should be aware of?
[09:06] Alex Monroe: From Redwood side we need sample prompts, a traffic profile, and confirm what data residency / KMS requirements exist. From your side maybe network controls for connecting to hosted endpoints in staging.
[09:18] Daniel Kim: We'll get those over.
[09:21] Priya Singh: I'll run the benchmark next week. We'll share the LangChain/LlamaIndex sample project in a repo.
[09:28] Maya Patel: Thanks, that sounds good.
[09:31] Alex Monroe: Ok I'll recap and send pricing/security docs. Thanks everyone.
[09:35] Daniel Kim: Thanks all.
[09:38] [END]
notes: Redwood to share LangChain & LlamaIndex example repo
